what: A lifting mechanism combines rotating links with screw-driven linear motion. A slewing frame and three screw actuators: leverage, self-locking and end-of-travel clutches.
try: Reset and run the example sequence.
Separate turntable motion from the lifting actuator’s motion.
Compare actuator extension with the height change at the end of the boom.
why: A screw turns rotation into a small linear displacement. The boom linkage then converts that stroke into an angle and tip height. Leverage varies with pose, so equal motor increments need not give equal tip-height increments.
matters: Cranes and excavators combine transmission and linkage geometry to handle loads.
question: Will doubling actuator extension always double boom-tip rise?
answer: No. The actuator is part of a changing triangle. Its angle and mechanical advantage vary with the pose.

formula: screw travel = turns × lead;  boom height also depends on linkage pose
